analysis.one_liner: Repeals the special law shielding gun makers and dealers from lawsuits over shootings.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the gun industry's special lawsuit shield was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2005, Congress passed a law — the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act — that blocks most lawsuits against gun manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for harm caused when their products are criminally misused. No other consumer industry has this shield. This bill would repeal it, letting victims of gun violence sue the industry like they could sue any other business, and would also let ATF gun-trace data be used as evidence in civil cases. The bill went to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved again; it got no vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who could sue manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations for damages from criminal misuse of a firearm, and courts and plaintiffs who could use ATF trace data to show how crime guns got to the street.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of gun violence and their families

how_it_helps.text: It would let victims of gun violence sue manufacturers, sellers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm — a path the 2005 law closed.
It would make ATF firearms trace data usable in civil cases, so plaintiffs and courts could see how specific dealers or manufacturers supplied guns later used in crimes.

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations, who would face civil lawsuits and the cost of defending them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Repealing the liability shield exposes gun companies to lawsuits over third-party criminal misuse, which the industry and its supporters argue could bankrupt domestic manufacturers and push gun production offshore or to less accountable actors.

Restoring liability for criminal misuse revives a form of litigation courts had blocked, and opponents argue it is a backdoor attempt to regulate firearms through lawsuits rather than through legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be a meaningful legal remedy for people harmed by guns and greater transparency about how crime guns reach the street. The costs are real but debatable: defendants facing lawsuits for third-party criminal acts are exposed to liability that does not depend on fault, and insurers could raise premiums or exit the market, and gun rights advocates argue this is a backdoor path to regulating firearms through litigation rather than legislation. Whether those suits would actually succeed is uncertain. The bill does not itself restrict gun ownership.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 22, 2021 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or other action followed; the complete action history ends with the committee referral.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill ever being reported out of committee, so it died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations keep the 2005 liability shield and remain largely untouchable in court for crimes committed with their products.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry, which kept its lawsuit shield

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied Independents.

for.name: 23 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without scheduling a hearing, markup, or vote; it never left the committee.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed repeal of the industry liability shield and lobbied against bills like this one.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never advanced past the committee stage.

industries.industry: Gun manufacturers, dealers, importers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, removing the unique liability shield that protects the industry from lawsuits over criminal misuse of its products, and lets ATF trace data be used against it in court. No other industry enjoys this statutory exemption from tort liability.
Reopened litigation over gun violence would generate new liability insurance and legal work, while insurers could raise premiums for gun industry clients.
